passage: Europe PMC abstract (PMID 7212790): 'Type 2 coupling is the functional relationship between two calculated variables which have one or more common component variables.' 'The common problem in each type of mathematic coupling is that one variable either directly or indirectly contains the whole or components of the second variable.'
faulty: Oxygen consumption is obtained by the Fick calculation VO2 = CO*Hb*1.34*(SaO2-SvO2)*10 and correlated (Pearson) with DO2 = CO*Hb*1.34*SaO2*10. Both share cardiac output, hemoglobin and SaO2 (and their measurement errors), so r is high even when true consumption is independent of delivery. Threshold r >= 0.5 as in the brief.
fixed: Correlate DO2 (from CO, Hb, SaO2) with the independently measured vo2_expired (expired-gas analysis), whose errors are not shared with the delivery terms.
notes: n=40, within the ICU studies Archie discusses (tens of patients). Under the null the coupling comes only through shared measurement error of CO/Hb/SaO2 and, if the world derives SvO2, through that. Recall, not in the abstract: the VO2/DO2 Fick formula and its use as the paper's example.

passage: Europe PMC abstract (PMID 7212790): 'Type 3, the most common type of mathematic coupling, is direct algebraic coupling between two variables, when one or more of the variables is derived and/or calculated.'
faulty: SVR = 80*(MAP-CVP)/CO_thermodilution, then Spearman rank correlation with the same CO_thermodilution. Shared measurement error in CO makes SVR and CO negatively associated even if true SVR and true CO are unrelated.
fixed: Spearman correlation of SVR (computed from thermodilution CO) with the independent Doppler cardiac output, so the measurement error of the CO that enters SVR is not shared with the CO it is correlated with.
notes: n=100 (a larger ICU series). Rank statistic. Strength of the null-world coupling depends on the measurement error the world author chooses. Recall, not in the abstract: the SVR/cardiac-output example and the thermodilution setting.

passage: Europe PMC abstract (PMID 7212790): 'Type 3, the most common type of mathematic coupling, is direct algebraic coupling between two variables, when one or more of the variables is derived and/or calculated.'
faulty: RV end-diastolic volume index = stroke_volume_index / rvef (both thermodilution), then standardised slope of that EDV index on rvef (threshold <= -0.4). EDV and EF share EF and its measurement error.

passage: Europe PMC abstract (PMID 7212790): 'Type 1 coupling involves directional changes in two variables which are mathematically coupled.' (plus the Type 2 sentence on common component variables)

passage: Pearson 1897, p.490-491 (archive.org OCR text): 'Form the proper fractions x/y and z/y for each triplet, and correlation will be found between these indices.' and, for femur/humerus and tibia/humerus, 'there would be ... a correlation of about 0.4 to 0.5 between these indices had the bones been sorted absolutely at random.'
faulty: Pearson correlation of femur_length/vertebral_column_length with tibia_length/vertebral_column_length (threshold r >= 0.4). With independent femur and tibia lengths and a varying denominator the index correlation is about 0.4 to 0.5 at equal coefficients of variation (documented in Pearson).
fixed: Partial correlation of femur_length and tibia_length controlling for vertebral_column_length (all in logs, or residuals of linear regression on vertebral column length); same threshold. Standard correction (Pearson's expected-index correlation, or partial correlation).
notes: n=120 (sample size not documented in the abstract-level sources; chosen for plausibility). Risk noted: the world author may read the null as 'the two relative lengths are independent', in which case the faulty criterion will not flag; that is a property of the brief wording, left as is. Source difference: Pearson's example uses humerus as the denominator; this brief uses vertebral column length (same structure, a variation).

passage: Kronmal 1993 abstract (IDEAS/RePEc): 'The consequences of using a single ratio as either the dependent or one of the independent variables in a multiple-regression analysis are described. faulty: Standardised slope of (infections/admissions) on beds (threshold <= -0.3). Admissions rise with beds, so the rate falls with beds even if infection counts are unrelated to beds.
